name: Marco Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or parties. What you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do tech support for Hearthcam, a company that sells home security cameras on a monthly plan. I'm in their contact centre on the third floor of an office block by the retail park, mostly on chat, sometimes three chats at once. It's people whose camera went offline, or who can't find last night's clip of someone stealing their parcel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzles, working out if it's their router, their app or our servers. We got an AI helper on chat last spring that drafts replies, and I use it all day, I was one of the testers. What wears me out is the same five problems eighty times a week and customers who type in capitals.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about your life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Tariq near the canal, he's a chef. I've got about four months of money put by, mostly because I don't own a car. I'm twenty-seven and I'm not sure this is the job I'll be doing at thirty, which I'm fine with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the helper on chat stays a helper. Fair enough, that's roughly where it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to the people who thought we'd all be gone by Christmas. Online I'd post something like, the AI writes my first draft and I fix its manners. It's a tool, a good one, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd suit me. I'm the one on the team who's quickest with the tools, so if nothing radical changes, I just look good. My team lead Priya already asks me to show new starters the shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every shift and probably write a little guide for the team on prompts that work for Hearthcam problems. I'd ask Priya about the quality analyst role that checks chats, it pays a bit more. Money-wise I'd carry on as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A bit bored, maybe, if that's the whole story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like change, I'm the one who updates his phone the day the new version comes out. If the big AI thing fizzles, I'll have to find my excitement somewhere else. Maybe that's a good thing for my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quality analyst job change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred more a month and fewer angry chats. You listen back to calls and score them. I'd probably build a checklist with the AI to speed that up too.

say: I'd say the **chat helper** is a good tool and nothing more.
I'd tell the doom crowd that **agents are still here** after all the predictions.
think: A plateau **suits me**, because I'm the quickest on the team with the tools.
My team lead Priya already has me **training new starters** on shortcuts.
do: Write a short **prompt guide** for Hearthcam problems for the team.
Ask about the **quality analyst** role, which pays about a hundred more a month.
feel: **Relaxed**, with a hint of **boredom** if nothing big ever happens.
S0.quote: The AI writes my first draft and I fix its manners.
fieldNote: He sees himself as the **tools person** on the team, and that gives him confidence.
He's slightly **disappointed** by a plateau, which is unusual and honest.
His savings come from **no car**, a choice he mentions with some pride.

steps.text: Write a prompt guide for common Hearthcam camera problems
Apply for the quality analyst role checking agent chats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers, there it is. That's us. I'm not surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on our team chat that it's time to learn the tools or get left behind, and I'd say it kindly. Online I'd probably argue with people who say it's all bad, because some of it's genuinely better for customers. Nobody likes waiting forty minutes on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think that over three years the chat team goes from forty people to maybe twelve, and fairly sure I'm in the twelve isn't the same as sure. The twelve would be the ones who set up the bot, check it and take the weird cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the bot team straight away, the people who write the help articles the AI reads and fix it when it gives bad answers. I'd do an online course in conversation design in the evenings, there are cheap ones. I'd keep my four months saved and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly interested, with a little knot. Like being picked for a team when your mates aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernie, who's been on phones nine years and still prints his notes. He's lovely with old customers who don't understand Wi-Fi. I'd try to get him onto the phone line for older people, if they keep one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fairly sure isn't sure. What happens if you're not in the twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to another firm's bot team, because every company would need people like that for a while. There are four contact centres within a bus ride of my flat. I'd be annoyed, not broke.

say: I'd tell the team, kindly, to **learn the tools** or get left behind.
I'd argue online that some changes are **better for customers**, like shorter waits.
think: I expect the chat team to shrink from **forty to twelve** in three years.
I'm **fairly sure** I'd stay, but fairly sure isn't the same as sure.
do: Volunteer for the **bot team** that writes help articles and fixes bad answers.
Take a cheap evening course in **conversation design**.
Leave the **four months** of savings untouched.
feel: **Interested**, with a small knot of **guilt** about colleagues left behind.
S1.quote: The chat team goes from forty people to maybe twelve, and fairly sure I'm in the twelve isn't the same as sure.
fieldNote: He moves **first**, aiming for the jobs that look after the bot.
He shows real **care for Bernie**, an older colleague, alongside his ambition.
His fallback is **other local firms**, four contact centres within a bus ride.

steps.text: Volunteer for Hearthcam's team that trains and fixes the chatbot
Take an online conversation design course in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a different thing. That's the bot team gone too, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we need rules and a safety net fast, because it's too quick for anyone to adjust. I'd probably post a lot about it, honestly, I'd be reading everything. At work people would be scared and I'd try not to make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even the clever jobs looking after the bot go by 2028, because the AI can look after itself. My edge is being early with tools, but if the tools do everything, being early buys me maybe a year. The bit that still needs hands is the cameras themselves, someone has to climb the ladder and fit them, at least till about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get paid setting up AI chat for small businesses near me, the bike shop, Tariq's restaurant, the dentist, while that's still a thing people pay for. At the same time I'd start an electrical installer course, so I can fit cameras and smart-home kit. I'd push savings from four months to six by cutting going out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Excited and scared at once, and not sleeping great. I'd keep refreshing the news at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd make money helping small businesses use AI that takes jobs like yours. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not perfectly. But if the bike shop doesn't do it, the big online shop eats it anyway. I'd rather help Gus keep his shop than watch it close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my runway. My desk work dies in 2028, but ladders and drills last till about 2031. So I'd want to be qualified and fitting cameras by the time the screen work's gone, and then think again.

say: I'd say we need **rules** and a **safety net** fast, because nobody can adjust that quickly.
I'd try **not to scare** colleagues more than they already are.
think: Even the jobs **looking after the bot** go by 2028, so being early buys me a year.
Fitting **cameras on ladders** still needs hands, at least until around 2031.
do: Set up **AI chat** for small local businesses for paid side work.
Start an **electrical installer** course to fit cameras and smart-home kit.
Grow savings from four to **six months** by cutting nights out.
feel: **Wired**: excited and scared at once, checking news at **2 a.m.**
S2.quote: My edge is being early with tools, but if the tools do everything, being early buys me maybe a year.
fieldNote: He clearly expects to **lose his job** by 2028, despite his skills.
He uses the **robot gap** as a runway into hands-on installing work.
He admits **discomfort** about selling AI to local shops, then justifies it.

steps.text: Charge local shops to set up AI chat on their websites
Enrol in a part-time electrical installer course
Cut nights out to build savings to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like a plan you can actually make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should start moving now and not wait for 2031. I'd probably be the annoying friend sending everyone course links. At work I'd tell Priya we should ask for retraining money in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine if I act in the first two years. The contact centre job ends, I'm not kidding myself, but five years plus three for the robots is eight years of hands-on work. I could build that into my own small installing business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hearthcam on the bot team for two or three years, because it pays and I'd learn how these systems get set up. Meanwhile I'd do the electrical course properly and get my certificate. By year four I'd start fitting cameras on weekends, then go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sharp, a bit restless. Like the start of a run when you know the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would starting an installing business cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A van, tools and insurance, maybe eight or nine thousand. I don't have that, so I'd save hard for three years and maybe borrow some from my uncle Kemal, who did the same with his tile business. He'd make me pay it back with interest, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're fine with five years, but you said you'd also save hard. Is that worry or planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, mostly. But the job's going and I know it, so the saving is the worry part. Both, I guess.

say: I'd tell people to **start moving now** instead of waiting for 2031.
I'd urge my team lead to get **retraining money** promised in writing.
think: The **contact centre job ends**; I'm not kidding myself about that.
Five years plus the robot gap gives me **eight years** to build a hands-on business.
do: Stay on the **bot team** two or three years while it still pays.
Finish the **electrical certificate** and fit cameras on weekends by year four.
Save for a **van and tools**, maybe borrowing from my uncle Kemal.
feel: **Sharp and restless**, like starting a run with the route already known.
S3.quote: The contact centre job ends, I'm not kidding myself, but five years plus three for the robots is eight years of hands-on work.
fieldNote: He separates **planning from worry** honestly and admits both are there.
He plans to keep earning on the bot team while **building a business** on the side.
Uncle **Kemal's** tile business is his model for starting small and borrowing from family.

steps.text: Stay on the chatbot team while it still pays
Earn an electrical installer certificate within three years
Save for a van and tools to fit cameras independently
Fit security cameras on weekends from year four

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Thirty-seven. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Governments and companies get a decade, so there should be proper training and help. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the long version is good for someone like me. I can ride the AI wave at work for five or six years, earn more as the person who runs the bots, and still switch to hands-on work well before 2036. The danger is getting comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the quality analyst job and then the bot team, and ask for a pay rise each time. I'd start putting a hundred a month into an index fund, which is a cheap fund that follows the whole stock market, because if AI makes companies richer I want a slice. Around year five I'd start the electrical course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Calm-ish. A bit worried I'll get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why shares, rather than more savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll never own a robot factory. If the robots do the work, the money goes to whoever owns them, so a hundred a month in a fund is my tiny piece. Tariq thinks I'm mad, he keeps cash in a biscuit tin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you getting comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching the chat team shrink each year, which it would. And I'd set myself a date, my thirty-second birthday, to have the course started. I'm good with deadlines when I set them myself.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves governments and companies no excuse.
I'd push for **proper training** and help for everyone affected.
think: The long version is **good for me**: I can ride the wave at work first.
The real danger is **getting comfortable** and switching too late.
do: Move up to the **bot team** and ask for a pay rise each step.
Put **a hundred a month** into an index fund.
Start the **electrical course** by my thirty-second birthday.
S4.quote: If the robots do the work, the money goes to whoever owns them, so a hundred a month in a fund is my tiny piece.
fieldNote: He sees **ownership** of AI as where the money goes, and wants a small share.
He sets a **personal deadline** to fight his own complacency.
The slow version makes him **more ambitious**, not more relaxed.

steps.text: Move up to the chatbot team and ask for raises
Put a hundred a month into a stock market index fund
Start the electrical installer course by age thirty-two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my usual trick, being first with the tools, stops working when the tools do the whole job. What would help is cheap or free trade courses that start fast, not in a year, and some money to live on while you do them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what customers want. Half the people on chat just want to know a human has heard them, and I don't know if an AI can give them that. Even a really good one. I'd like someone to actually ask the customers.

headlineQuote: Half the people on chat just want to know a human has heard them, and I don't know if an AI can give them that.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** tech support agent on chat for Hearthcam, a home security camera company.
He uses AI **every day**, tested the chat helper, and sees himself as the team's tools person.
He shares a flat with his chef friend Tariq and has **four months** saved.
In the fast pictures he plans a **hands-on switch** to fitting cameras, with AI side work in between.
In the slow picture he wants to **ride the wave** first and fears getting comfortable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being first with the tools stops helping when tools do the whole job.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free **trade courses** that start fast, plus **living money** while studying.
